From CAD to a Rolling Prototype

The build followed one continuous thread — a reference study, a surface model, a hand-built seat pattern, a mould taken off that pattern, cast parts, and a fully assembled show bike.

1
Benchmarking
Starting from a real reference vehicle

Before any surface was drawn, we benchmarked proportions, seat height, and panel-split logic against a real production scooter — grounding the show bike's ambitious styling in dimensions and ergonomics that actually work on a rider.

2
CAD Surfacing
Building the show bike's surfaces in UG NX

The body, seat, and panel surfaces were developed in UG NX as a full synchronous-modeling assembly, colour-coded by body region so panel splits, parting lines, and mounting bosses could be reviewed and iterated with the design lead before a single piece of tooling was cut.

3
Seat Pattern
Hand-building the seat's master pattern

The seat surface from CAD was translated into a physical master pattern, shaped and finished by hand to the exact profile and mounting-boss positions from the model — top surface and understructure both built to take a mould impression directly off this pattern.

4
Seat Moulding
Casting the two-part seat mould

A two-part mould was cast directly off the master pattern, capturing the full seat profile, hem line, and boss locations as a negative. This mould became the tooling used to lay up the actual seat shells — the step that turns a one-off hand pattern into a repeatable part.

5
Prototype Parts
Pulling the first cast seat shells

The first fibreglass seat shells came out of the mould — top skin and understructure — and were checked against the CAD surface for shrinkage, wall thickness, and boss alignment before being trimmed and prepped for fitment on the bike.

6
Full Build
Assembly, and the finished show-floor build

Body panels, the moulded seat, and the running gear came together into the full-scale prototype — first in primer-grey and cream for fit and finish review with the team, then refined into the show-ready build with painted panels, wheels, and lighting fitted.

7
Show Day
The finished machine, painted and badged

The final handoff: fully painted body panels in the show livery, the moulded seat trimmed and fitted, wheels and running gear installed, and the "TANTO" badging applied — the same surface that started as a synchronous-modeling assembly in UG NX, now standing as a complete, show-floor-ready motorcycle.

The Challenge

Show-floor finish on a compressed timeline

A tech show build gets judged on sight before anyone touches it, but the seat and body panels still needed to survive repeated handling, transport, and reassembly at the venue — all inside a timeline set by the show date, not the design process.

Approach

Parallel-tracking aesthetics, structure, and the vendor chain

I kept surface and structural work moving together rather than sequentially, so a styling change never meant restarting a structural check from zero — and kept the pattern, mould, and prototyping vendors moving in step with that same CAD timeline so tooling was never waiting on a design decision, or vice versa.

  • Modeled seat and body panel surfaces in UG NX and Fusion 360, iterating quickly on styling with the design lead's feedback.
  • Checked panel mounting points and seat frame against structural loads expected from handling and transport, not just static display.
  • Took the design through pattern, mould, and cast-part stages, confirming fit, finish, and panel-to-panel gaps matched CAD intent at every handoff.
  • Coordinated with the fabrication team to compress the prototype-to-show timeline without skipping validation steps.
Design for Prototype

Designing parts the way a prototype shop actually builds them

Because every panel and the seat shell were going to be pattern-built and hand-laid rather than injection tooled, the CAD was developed with Design for Prototype in mind from the start — generous draft on pattern faces, split lines placed where a mould could realistically part, and boss and rib features sized for hand lay-up rather than high-pressure tooling. That upfront discipline is what let the pattern-to-mould-to-part sequence above run in one pass instead of several.

Program Ownership

Vendor coordination, development, costing, and project management

Beyond the CAD and physical build, I ran the program side of this project end to end — from planning the CAD-to-show-floor schedule backward from a fixed show date, to owning every vendor conversation and cost decision that got the seat and panels from a surface model to a real part in hand.

Vendor Coordination
Ran day-to-day coordination with the pattern-maker, mould shop, and fabrication team, syncing hand-offs at each of the six stages shown above so no vendor was ever idle waiting on another.
Vendor Development
Identified and onboarded pattern and moulding vendors suited to a one-off, hand-built prototype rather than production tooling, and worked with them through their first pass on this geometry.
Costing
Owned part and process costing across pattern, mould, and cast-part stages, keeping the prototype build within the program's allocated budget as scope firmed up.
Project Planning
Built the CAD-to-show-floor schedule backward from the fixed show date, sequencing pattern, mould, casting, and assembly so structural checks never got skipped to save time.
Project Management
Tracked progress against that schedule day to day, resolving fit and finish issues as they surfaced at each handoff and re-sequencing work when a stage ran long.
Design for Prototype
Detailed panel and seat geometry for pattern-and-mould construction specifically — draft, split lines, and rib sizing chosen for hand lay-up rather than production tooling.
Outcome

A validated build, delivered on schedule

The seat and body panel prototypes reached the show floor with both the finish quality the display required and the structural integrity to survive handling — completed on a shortened development timeline, with every vendor handoff and cost line tracked from the first CAD surface to the finished bike.

Key Takeaway

"On a show build, the panel still has to be engineered — it just also has to be beautiful under the lights. Getting there on schedule is as much about the vendor chain as it is about the CAD."
